1	# The compiled checker, the code generator and the run time
     2	
     3	**count stage**
     4	: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library and prints its errors: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total, the checker count, counts the errors up to each component's first error.
     5	
     6	The code of this area is in these directories:
     7	
     8	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
     9	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
    10	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
    11	
    12	The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.
    13	
    14	## What the two paths share
    15	
    16	After the phases, each path has its own code for these:
    17	
    18	- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
    19	- Number natives: walk's `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`), and the compiled `nativeHelpers/` (`simpleIntArith.java`).
    20	- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
    21	- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.
    22	
    23	The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.
    24	
    25	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
    26	
    27	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.
    28	
    29	Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay.
    30	
    31	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
    32	
    33	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
    34	
    35	- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
    36	- a local function declaration, and an object expression;
    37	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.
    38	
    39	It also refuses a function, method, object or trait declaration with a `where` clause of its own, and a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose `extends` entry has a `where` clause. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private` and `abstract`, such as `override` (ledger row 650).
    40	
    41	The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
    42	
    43	Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).
    44	
    45	## What the code generator does
    46	
    47	`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time", gives the jars, the dispatch methods, the templates and the boxed numbers.
    48	
    49	- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
    50	- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
    51	- The `value` modifier has no effect on the representation.
    52	- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet (`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time"). If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):
    53	
    54	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'
    55	
    56	## The run time
    57	
    58	- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
    59	- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches.
    60	
    61	## Natives
    62	
    63	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
    64	
    65	The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method.
    66	
    67	## Traps of the compiled path
    68	
    69	- Before disambiguation, the compiled path bounds an unbounded type parameter by `Object`, not `Any`. Walk does not. So the compiled path rejects every generic that is instantiated at a tuple type, until the switch-over (ledger row 412).
    70	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
    71	- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. The team turned it off in 2012 (`c35aac139`). If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
    72	
    73	## The `fortress` commands
    74	
    75	`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
    76	
    77	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
    78	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
    79	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
    80	- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.
    81	
    82	## Running
    83	
    84	    cd ProjectFortress
    85	    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    86	    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    87	    ../bin/fortress run P [args]
    88	
    89	A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.
    90	
    91	- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
    92	- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead: it gives the cause.
    93	
    94	## Before an edit
    95	
    96	Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. Both date from September 2026, so a status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.
    97	
    98	- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.
    99	
   100	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'
   101	
   102	- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the run time and B.12 the natives.
   103	
   104	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'
   105	
   106	- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.
   107	
   108	## Testing an edit here
   109	
   110	- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. This takes seconds, rebuilds nothing and changes nothing tracked. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:
   111	
   112	      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
   113	      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java
   114	      rm -rf $Q/caches && cp -a default_repository/caches $Q/caches
   115	      java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "$Q/classes:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile P.fss
   116	      bin/fortress run P
   117	
   118	  For a Scala file, compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d $Q/classes -encoding UTF-8 X.scala`. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
   119	- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).
   120	
   121	## The checker's time
   122	
   123	This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.
   124	
   125	The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about a minute. It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.
   126	
   127	The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:
   128	
   129	- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
   130	- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.
   131	
   132	A node's hash starts from its class's name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks or a union's members, moves only where the change itself moves it. Such a move is a difference: keep the old order, or report the difference, as for any other.
   133	
   134	`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node, so one long walker method slows the whole checker. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.
   135	
   136	The timing is a smoke test. It is there to catch a slowdown of several times, or of orders of magnitude: a change that makes the checker three times slower must show. One run of each tree is enough. A small difference, or one within the noise from run to run, is not a finding. In your report, say what you saw, and do not analyse it.
   137	
   138	If you change the checker:
   139	
   140	1. Make the change correct, with its tests. Commit it, and name the commit in your report.
   141	2. Time the base build and the change, named `base` and `change`. Run the base in a call set up for the base build (`build-and-caches.md`), and the change in a call set up for your tree, each in the background (`session.md`). Use the same command for both, with `N` the run's name:

1	# The library
     2	
     3	The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:
     4	
     5	- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
     6	- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
     7	- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
     8	- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.
     9	
    10	## How loops and reductions call the library
    11	
    12	The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:
    13	
    14	- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
    15	- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
    16	- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.
    17	
    18	These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.
    19	
    20	## The curator's decisions on the library
    21	
    22	- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
    23	- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
    24	- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
    25	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. If the generators and the body do not fix the element type, write it, also where a declared type receives the value: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
    26	- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.
    27	
    28	## Designing a change
    29	
    30	- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
    31	- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
    32	- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
    33	- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
    34	- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
    35	- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
    36	- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
    37	- A new native is a Java class under `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"), so it is an edit of walk's Java too.
    38	- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.
    39	
    40	## Editing
    41	
    42	A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.

1	# The interpreter (walk)
     2	
     3	Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:
     4	
     5	- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
     6	- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
     7	- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
     8	- `glue/`: the natives.
     9	
    10	## How walk evaluates a program
    11	
    12	After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.
    13	
    14	At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.
    15	
    16	Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.
    17	
    18	## Where a fix of walk belongs
    19	
    20	Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:
    21	
    22	- coercion;
    23	- chained comparisons;
    24	- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
    25	- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
    26	- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.
    27	
    28	Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if walk is wrong on one of these nodes, fix the evaluator, not the desugarer.
    29	
    30	An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.
    31	
    32	## What walk checks
    33	
    34	Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiler's prelude and the compiled path's desugaring switches (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program, and `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
    35	
    36	At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It refuses:
    37	
    38	- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it loads the pair only if the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the return-type rule hold on their declared domains, except in the cases that `revival-changes.md` lists. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes, so such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail. `revival-changes.md`, "Walk's check of two generic declarations", defines the declared domain and lists those cases.
    39	- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`) in a type that provides both.
    40	- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
    41	- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses.
    42	- an object or object expression without static parameters that inherits an abstract method and does not define it. Bodies define it if they are at or below its parameter types and together cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk also refuses where its search for a cover does not settle: at a cycle of `comprises` clauses, at a symbolic type, or beyond 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations of listed types. It also refuses a valid object whose one body for the method has a static parameter of its own (ledger row 728).
    43	- a declaration with the modifier `override`, in a trait, object or object expression, that overrides no declaration that its type's immediate supertraits provide. An `override` at an inherited declaration's own parameter types overrides nothing. At an instance of a generic trait above a declared object, equal parameter types count as overridden. Walk does not read all the bounds of the static parameters in two cases:
    44	  - an object expression, which takes its static parameters from the function around it;
    45	  - a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause.
    46	
    47	  In these cases, walk does not refuse an `override` if the inherited declaration's parameter types mention a static parameter and differ from the `override`'s.
    48	
    49	So a library edit can stop every program at load, if it does one of these:
    50	
    51	- adds an overload;
    52	- leaves an inherited abstract method that no bodies cover, covers it only by a body with a static parameter of its own, or covers it by bodies whose cover walk's search cannot settle;
    53	- adds an `override` that overrides nothing.
    54	
    55	`tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.
    56	
    57	Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.
    58	
    59	## Natives
    60	
    61	The library binds each of walk's natives by a string in its `.fss` files: `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X")`. The classes are in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. They take the evaluator's boxed values, so the compiled path cannot use them. `import java`, the compiled path's way to bind natives, is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it.
    62	
    63	To raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees, a native throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `Int.java` there makes one, and its callers throw it:
    64	
    65	    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
    66	    return new FortressError(f);
    67	
    68	A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other exception from a native ends the run, a division by zero too.
    69	
    70	## Running a program
    71	
    72	    bin/fortress P.fss
    73	
    74	- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
    75	- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
    76	- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
    77	- Your setup sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, the size of the pool, to 1 (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"). If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs.
    78	- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches.
    79	- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.
    80	- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss`. It prints `SUM[i <- 1#100] i = 5050` among its lines, and exits 0. `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.
    81	
    82	## The model program
    83	
    84	MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. The script runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from an empty private cache and writes `<work-dir>/<name>.txt`. Read its `VERDICT:` line and its last line, `rc=`.
    85	
    86	- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.
    87	- If you change a line of the model, put the change in your report as a diff.

content.content:
- F-174 **The specification states the type group's 2011 overloading model: declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters, and a declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration over all its instances within its bounds.** It states P-45 and P-42. The section "Declarations with Static Parameters" states the OOPSLA 2011 paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet. It gives one more restriction as the compiled path's, not the language's. Where one generic declaration is more specific than another with as many static parameters, the two must declare them of the same kinds, position by position. Also, the more specific one's return type must be a subtype of the other's when their static parameters are matched by position, so the checker refuses an override whose return type reorders its static parameters (row 398, fixed). The section "Principles of Overloading" forbids overloading a functional whose single parameter's type is a type parameter with the bound `Any` written, as `T extends Any`. A type parameter with no `extends` clause, whose bound is also `Any`, is exempt. Both paths refuse such an overload: the checker in `OverloadingChecker.checkBoundAny`, and walk since row 534's fix. Neither path runs every set that the rules allow. Appendix I's entry "Overloading with static parameters" names the sets that each path fails. In row 542, the checker refuses a generic declaration beside a plain one over an object type, as `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: Circle): Circle`. In row 537, the code generator fails on two generic declarations whose bounds differ. In row 539, walk refuses at load the 2019 paper's valid set over an array list and a list. In rows 779 and 780, walk fails on two generic functional methods one of whose declared domains lies inside the other's: in a trait or object without static parameters it refuses them at load, and in a trait with static parameters it loads them, but a call to which both apply fails. Detail: `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:134-150` and `:531-674`; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 3 and 4.
- F-50 **The compiled checker lets overloads differ in static parameters, as the model of the OOPSLA 2011 paper does, which the specification now states (F-174); as ambiguous, it refuses only the pairs it cannot prove unambiguous.** It builds P-45. It cannot prove a pair over open traits, which no `excludes` or `comprises` clause closes, nor one whose domains exclude only through the exclusion rule and a bound, as the library's `CAP` on `ScalarRange[\I\]` beside `Range2D[\I,J\]` does. It also refuses some pairs that the paper accepts, by its Return Type Rule and by its positional rule, under which two generic declarations in the more-specific relation agree on their static parameters by position (F-75). Other gaps have their own owners: its overloading check never reads a pair of symbolic operators such as `+` (P-155, row 584); two generic arms on a bare type variable fail compiled (F-174, row 537); and walk runs an arm whose size the call leaves unfixed, with the size unbound, where the checker drops the arm or refuses the call (F-69, row 400). Detail: `reviews/overload-static-params-ways.md` sections 2 and 3.
- F-75 **The compiled checker checks the Return Type Rule over every instance, and a positional rule: when two generic declarations in the more-specific relation declare as many static parameters of their own, those parameters agree in kind by position, and the more specific return type is a subtype of the other once the other's parameters are read as its own by position.** The equal-count scope and the comparison of kinds are the rung's choices. It builds P-45. Checking every instance, as P-45 asks, it also refuses a generic declaration beside a plain one whose domain is an object type, a pair that the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`) accepts, since the paper sets aside the instances whose domains cannot meet (row 542, open). In the interpreter's library the two rules refuse no pair: the distance holds no return-type or overloading error (F-53). Gated by `compiler_tests/OverloadGeneric*` and `OverloadBoundNamesForced`, which accept; `XXXOverloadReturnEveryInstance` and `XXXOverloadPermutedStaticParams`, which pin the two rules' refusals; and `XXXOverloadReturnObjectDomain`, which pins row 542's. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-return-type-rule/decision-record.md` sections 1 and 2.
- F-223 **The specification's No Duplicates Rule is the papers' non-strict rule, and the compiled checker applies it, to functional methods wherever their `self` parameters stand, abstract ones included.** Two declarations of one name may not each be applicable to every call to which the other is, as in the type group's papers of 2011 and 2019 (P-26). The checker refuses such a pair, two functional methods at different `self` positions and an abstract functional method beside a concrete one among them: "There are multiple declarations of f with the same parameter type", naming the domain of the declaration written first. It checks no symbolic operator (row 584); such a pair passes it and stops the code generator (row 726). Walk refuses at load such a pair of two generic declarations whose parameter types mention their static parameters, as `dup[\T\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `dup[\U\](x: Box[\U\])`; it refuses too a generic declaration beside one whose parameter types are its bounds, a plain one or a generic one whose parameter types mention none of its static parameters, 'fails because their parameter lists have the same types'. Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXNoDuplicatesRule`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositions`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsPlain`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstract` and `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstractSelfPositions`, the checker's departure by `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsOperator`, walk's refusal by `tests/NoDuplicatesRuleWalk`, and those two refusals by `tests/GenericBesidePlainSameDomain` and `GenericBesideGenericSameDomain`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-popl-examples/REPORT.md` section 4, its `SKEPTIC.md` section 2, `compile-ladder/rung-duplicates-coverage/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 8, and `compile-ladder/rung-checker-abstract-callsite/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-26 **Under walk, when one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, the call chooses on their declared domains where exactly one lies inside the other, not by the order in which they are written.** It builds P-45, the choice among overloads by declared parameter types, under walk. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, where each lies inside the other, or where neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance, and a generic dotted method is chosen by F-253 (a generic method at a dotted call, also chosen on declared domains). If the chosen declaration is generic and its instance takes an argument only by a conversion, walk converts the argument and dispatches the converted arguments again, so the most specific declaration for the converted values runs. In two cases walk keeps the chosen instance, with no second dispatch: an overloaded dotted method, and a position whose conversion `Coercions.coercionFor` does not find, such as a tuple converted element by element. Two generic overloads whose static parameters agree in name, kind and bounds share one symbolic instance, even if their `where` clauses differ; no test or library declaration has such a pair (row 478). Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss` and `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.1, 5.2 (the second dispatch) and 5.5 (the symbolic instance).
- F-27 **Walk's load check reads again two kinds of overload pair that its parameter-by-parameter check refuses, and accepts those that pass: a generic declaration beside a plain one, read on their declared domains, and two plain top-level functions, not methods, whose overlap other declarations cover through `comprises` clauses.** To test a cover, the check cuts the overlap of the two domains, position by position, into parts by the `comprises` clauses. Each combination of parts must lie inside the domain of one declaration without static parameters that lies below both. So several such declarations may together cover the overlap. A search that does not settle refuses. A generic declaration beside a plain one passes where one declared domain lies strictly inside the other and the inner one's return type lies below the outer one's. Where neither lies inside the other, the pair needs the same cover, or declared domains that exclude each other read whole (F-258, exclusion over the whole parameter type). Equal declared domains are refused. It builds under walk P-46, by which a conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, and P-60, by which several declarations below both may cover a meet. Two generic declarations are read on their declared domains too (F-252: the No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet Rules, each over its own instances). Walk still refuses the valid example of the POPL 2019 paper on symmetric multiple dispatch (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`, p. 11:13), a set of three generic declarations (row 539). Gated by `tests/ComprisesMeetWalk.fss` and `GenericBesidePlain*.fss`, among others. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.3 (generic beside plain) and 5.4 (the cover).
- F-252 **Under walk, where the parameter-by-parameter check refuses two declarations with static parameters of their own, the load check reads the pair again on its declared domains, by the No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet Rules.** A declaration with static parameters of its own is a generic function, a generic object's constructor, or a functional method that declares static parameters in a trait or object that has none. Walk's load check first compares two overloads parameter by parameter, and a pair that it finds excluding loads. It reads a refused pair of two such declarations again, each over all its own instances, and loads the pair if it meets the three rules. A pair that the parameter check orders is read again only for the No Duplicates Rule (F-274). F-275 holds the Return Type Rule. The parameter check does not find two instances of one generic type at different ground static arguments excluding, such as `Tg[\3\]` and `Tg[\4\]`, so two plain declarations so typed are refused (row 416). For the Meet Rule, walk looks for a third declaration that covers the overlap only where, at each position, the two parameter types are equal, or one of them is a static parameter, or both are instances of one generic type whose static arguments match in the same way (row 539). A pair whose domains exclude when read whole also loads, where neither declaration has a `where` clause of its own (F-258; row 787). A pair with a varargs parameter is not read again and keeps the parameter check's refusal (F-257). At a call, walk compares a functional method of a generic trait or object on the instance that the call makes. It compares a generic dotted method in the same way, except where exactly one of the two declared domains lies inside the other; there it chooses the inner one (F-253). Gated by `tests/DispatchRenamedGenericArmWalk`, `DispatchSwappedGenericArmWalk` and `GenericPairNestedBoundsWalk` (load and dispatch), and the expected failure `XXXOverloadExistentialMeetWalk` (row 539). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-generic-pairs/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 5.
- F-257 **Under walk, a pair of declarations that the load check refuses after it reads the pair on its declared domains is refused in the name of the rule that the pair breaks.** The load check reads a pair on its declared domains where its parameter-by-parameter check refuses the pair and both declarations have static parameters of their own, or one has them and the other is a plain declaration (F-252, F-27). It reads a pair that the check orders only for the No Duplicates Rule (F-274). The Return Type Rule: "fails the Return Type Rule: the first [second] is more specific, and its return type is not found to be a subtype of the return type of every instance of the second [first] that applies to its arguments". The Meet Rule: "fails the Meet Rule: neither is found to be more specific than the other or to exclude it, and no declaration is found that is more specific than both and applies to every call to which both apply". The No Duplicates Rule: walk's "fails because their parameter lists have the same types". The messages say "not found" because walk's reading is narrower than the rules: rows 539, 550, 416 and 779 hold valid pairs that walk refuses. A pair that is not read on its declared domains keeps the parameter check's message, such as "with generic type, at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types". Such a pair has a varargs parameter, or parameter lists of different lengths, or raises an error while its instances are read. Or it is of neither kind above, as a functional method of a generic trait beside another, or it is the pair of instances that an explicit instantiation such as `f[\A, B\]` makes of two generic declarations of one name (`XXXGenericOverload2`). The message does not decide which pairs load. Gated by `tests/GenericReturnRuleInvariantWalk`, `GenericReturnRuleOuterParamWalk` and `GenericBesidePlainReturnRuleWalk` (Return Type), `GenericOverloadInstancesApartWalk`, `GenericBoundsNoMeetWalk` and `GenericBesidePlainNoMeetWalk` (Meet), and `NoDuplicatesRuleWalk` and `NoDuplicatesRuleSizeWalk` (No Duplicates). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-trait-method-bounds/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 3.

content.content:
- F-274 **Under walk, two declarations whose declared domains are equal are refused by the No Duplicates Rule, where one has static parameters of its own and the other has its own or none, whether or not the parameter-by-parameter check orders them.** The parameter check reads a type parameter as strictly below its bound. So it orders `h[\T extends Number\](x: T, y: T)` before `h(x: Number, y: Number)`, though their declared domains are equal. Walk compares the declared domains, each declaration's over all its own instances, and refuses the pair: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types" (F-257). A type parameter bounded by `Any` counts: walk refuses `g[\T\](a: T)` beside `g(a: Any)`, and the compiled checker accepts that pair (row 759). Gated by `tests/GenericBesideGenericSameDomain`, `GenericBesidePlainSameDomain`, `NoDuplicatesRuleWalk` and `NoDuplicatesRuleSizeWalk` (refused). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-generic-pairs/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 5; `compile-ladder/rung-existential-reduction/REPORT.md` section 5 (row 759 on both paths).
- F-275 **Under walk, where the parameter-by-parameter check refuses two declarations with static parameters of their own and one lies inside the other, the load check reads the Return Type Rule at one instance of the outer one, and refuses the pair unless that instance stands for every instance that applies.** The instance is the one that walk's inference finds for the outer one at the inner one's parameter types. A check at that instance alone would load pairs that the rule refuses, since an argument of the inner one can select a smaller instance of the outer one. The instance stands for every applicable instance in two cases. In the first, each static parameter that the outer one's return type names is fixed by a static argument of one of its parameter types. In the second, the outer one returns one of its own type parameters, and the inner one meets one of two conditions. Either it returns a type parameter of its own that is the whole type of at least one of its parameters and appears in no other parameter type than those at positions where the outer one's parameter type is that returned type parameter; or, at such a position, it has an object type below which its return type lies. Otherwise walk refuses the pair, "fails the Return Type Rule" (F-257). With `trait Shape`, `trait Round extends Shape` and `object Circle extends Round`, it refuses `f[\T extends Shape\](x: T, y: T): T` beside `f[\U extends Round\](x: U, y: Round): Round`, and `f[\T extends Shape\](x: T): Box[\T\]` beside `f[\U extends Round\](x: U): Box[\U\]`; the compiled checker refuses both too. Gated by `tests/GenericReturnRuleOuterParamWalk` and `GenericReturnRuleInvariantWalk` (refused) and `GenericReturnRuleHoldsWalk` (load and dispatch). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-generic-pairs/SKEPTIC.md` section 2.
- F-238 **Under walk's load check, an exclusion that two declarations with static parameters of their own show only when each is read at a symbolic instantiation is withdrawn where their instances do not exclude.** A declaration with static parameters of its own is defined in F-252. The check first reads two generic functions of one name and one list of static parameters at one shared symbolic instantiation, and two instances of one generic object as two object types that cannot be extended, so they exclude. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\])`, with `trait P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, excludes at one `T`, though a type that extends `P[\ZZ32\]` and `Q[\String\]` has both. Walk then reads such an exclusion again over the instances of each. Instances of one generic type exclude only where their static arguments cannot be equal. Any other exclusion stands where the two still exclude with their static parameters renamed apart. Or, read at the shared instantiation, it stands where every generic type that both extend forces their static arguments to be equal, since no type extends two instances of one generic trait: so `Array` and `ImmutableArray` exclude at every pair of instances through `ReadableArray`. A pair whose exclusion is withdrawn goes on to the reading on declared domains (F-252), and a refusal there names the rule that the pair breaks (F-257). Gated, as refusals at load, by `tests/GenericBoundsNoMeetWalk`, `NoDuplicatesRuleWalk`, `NoDuplicatesRuleSizeWalk` and `GenericOverloadInstancesApartWalk`; as programs that load, by `GenericBoundsMeetWalk`, `GenericFBoundsMeetWalk`, `GenericPairExcludingWalk`, `GenericSizePairNestedWalk`, `ShuffleTest` and `GenericPairExcludesTogetherWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-overload-if/REPORT.md` section 1, "Row 373", and section 9.
- F-258 **Walk and the compiled checker read exclusion between two declarations, one or both with static parameters, over the whole parameter type, by existential reduction.** A value of both declared domains has, at each position, one instance of each generic type that the two parameter types there are or extend, so those instances' static arguments are equal; the two domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where, at the instance they force, the parameter types at some position exclude. Walk: the Meet branches of `genericPairValid` and of `validOnDeclaredDomains`'s generic-beside-plain reading also ask `domainsExcludeTogether` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:935` at `a93fb3bfd`), which reads bounds where `mayBeEqual` and `meetParams` read them and reads no `where` clause, varargs or lists of different lengths; at the instance the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter apart only where they cannot meet at any instance of it: an object type apart from a type that neither it nor a supertype of it may be, and no `comprises` clause (`excludesAtMeet`, `OverloadedFunction.java:1041` at `84957e6ef`). The checker: `OverloadingOracle.excludes` asks `TypeSchemaAnalyzer.emptyED` beside `subtypeED` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:326`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:444`): the existential reduction's first premise alone, its bounds not read. On the interpreter's library `emptyED` is never reached: `subtypeED` shows all 691 meets the count stage tests empty. The two paths differ on two type parameters whose bounds exclude (row 786); on such a pair one of whose declarations has a `where` clause, which walk refuses and the checker accepts (row 787); and on a pair that walk's parameter check reads apart, reading an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type it is at some instance, as `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which walk loads and the checker refuses (row 788). Gated by `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericPairExcludesTogetherWalk`, `GenericPairForcedObjectApartWalk`, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/GenericPairExcludesTogether` and `GenericPairSharedSupertypeExclusion` (load, compile and dispatch), and `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericPairFreeArgumentWalk`, `GenericPairObjectSupertypeOverlapWalk` and `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXGenericPairFreeArgument` (refused). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-existential-reduction/REPORT.md` sections 2, 5 and 7.
- F-253 **Under walk, a call of a generic method that writes no static argument infers the method's own static arguments from the arguments' run-time types.** This holds for a dotted call, as for a call of a generic function, whether the method is alone under its name or among its receiver's overloads. Among the receiver's overloads, where one of two is a generic dotted method and exactly one of their declared domains lies inside the other, walk chooses the inner one; otherwise it compares them on the instance that the call makes (F-252). A generic method that a trait declares reads its bounds, and the types to which its arguments convert, in the trait's method environment, where its instances bind and evaluate their types, as a method that an object declares does. So it takes the instance that the same method declared in an object takes: a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` give `Box[\ZZ64\]` with the `ZZ32` converted, and a bounded type parameter that nothing fixes takes its bound. A generic functional method that an object inherits from a trait is chosen beside the object's plain one where only it applies. Where the inference with conversion finds no instance, as for an argument outside a bound, walk falls back to unification. For a trait's method, the unification still reads the trait's member environment, which has no parent, as the team's code did. So it does not read the bound, and the call fails with 'Cannot unify Int ... with Shape ... abm=K=(Int,Any)'; the same method declared in an object fails with 'Meet(Int, Shape) not a singleton'. This inference lets the team's generic `distribute` over `K` run nested reductions under walk (F-248). Gated by `tests/MethodStaticArgInference.fss`, `MethodStaticArgOverloadedReceiver.fss`, `MethodStaticArgDeclaredDomain.fss`, `NestedReductionFusion.fss`, `TraitGenericMethodInference.fss` and `InheritedGenericFunctionalMethodBesidePlain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-method-sargs/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 2; `compile-ladder/rung-walk-trait-method-bounds/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 4, and its `SKEPTIC.md` section 3.
- P-45 **Overloaded declarations may differ in their static parameters.** The specification drops its sentence that forbids this, and keeps it as superseded text. It states instead the overloading model of the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which the compiled checker already used. The checker keeps the paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type. It checks the Return Type Rule over every instance of a generic declaration that the argument types allow, not over one guessed instance. One rule of the old sentence survives: if one generic declaration is more specific than another, their static parameters must line up position by position, as Java's rule for overriding a generic method requires. Walk chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declaration declares, not by the order in which they are written. At load, walk judges each pair of two generic declarations by the checker's rules on their declared parameter types. It does not refuse a pair only because none of their parameter types exclude, as when one declaration is more specific than the other. Walk and the checker must accept the same pairs. The library repairs, by declarations of its own, the overload sets that the checker refused, and no line of microGPT's two programs changes. Where walk or the checker still judges a pair against these rules: walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on the instance that a call makes (F-26); both paths refuse the paper's own valid example (row 539); walk refuses two nested generic functional methods of a plain trait, and fails at a call on them in a generic trait (rows 779 and 780); and walk and the checker disagree on four kinds of pair (rows 759 and 786 to 788).
- P-152 **Walk and the compiled checker read the exclusion of two generic declarations over their whole parameter types, by existential reduction.** With static parameters, the parameter types of two declarations can exclude each other as a whole, even where no single parameter excludes its counterpart. In `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, where `P[\T\]` excludes `Q[\T\]` only at the same `T`, neither parameter excludes alone. But no value is a `Box` of two types, so `b` fixes the same `T` for both declarations, and no argument fits both. A generic trait in `Box`'s place fixes `T` in the same way. Both paths read such a pair as excluding, and judge it on that reading by the overloading rules (P-45: the 2011 paper's No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type rules). Why: the type group's 2011 paper decides exclusion between parameter types with static parameters by existential reduction (`Papers/Types/exc-reduction.tick`; P-26, the type group's later word outweighs the specification's early text), as the revised specification states (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Declarations with Static Parameters"). Walk refuses such a pair at load where one declaration has a `where` clause, which the checker accepts (row 787); and walk reads an object type over a static parameter, such as `Box[\T\]`, as excluding a type that it equals at some instance, such as `Box[\ZZ32\]`, so that it loads a pair that the checker refuses (row 788).
- P-149 **An object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait, and a body for it from a sibling trait, is refused unless it declares the method itself.** In `object O extends { A, B }`, where `A` declares `pick(self)` abstract and `B` gives `pick(self)` a body, `O` must declare its own `pick`. Scala's way, where the sibling trait's body implements the abstract method, is not taken. The compiled checker refuses such an object, as the specification's text and the type group's Welterweight calculus (`Papers/Welterweight/`) require. Walk already refuses it at load, by the Meet Rule for Functional Methods. A trait that declares one method both abstract and with a body, at the same parameter types, is refused too. Why: the revival honors the designers' intent. It changes Fortress's nature only to reconcile a conflict between the earlier and the later designers' choices, and then looks to other languages for how to do it. Here there is no such conflict, and Fortress is not bent to Scala's way for a hypothetical convenience.

# Fortress gap ledger

The gap ledger records, one claim to a row, where the revival's tree departs from Fortress as its specification and the team's papers describe it: what fails, what works that a source doubted, and what a source claimed wrongly. Each row carries its status, its kind and area, the specification's word on it, a reproducer, and who found it; the open rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A row keeps its number for good, wherever it sits: a fixed or repeated row becomes one line in its place, and the full earlier line of every changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read a row with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'ledger:N'`, and find rows with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'ledger-find:WORDS'`; do not read this file whole. Write it only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` (`add FILE --section TITLE`, `note`, `rewrite N FILE`, `close`, `duplicate`), which checks every line it writes against the template below and keeps the history; `ledger.py count` prints the counts by status, kind and area, `ledger.py check` lints the whole file, and `ledger.py landing-check BASE` runs the checks of a landing since BASE.

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITION
139:| 416 | **walk's overloading check applies no instantiation exclusion**: it refuses `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, "first parameters b:[Tg[\4\]] and b:[Tg[\3\]] are unrelated", the type twin, and overloads on two traits extending `Tg[\3\]` and `Tg[\4\]`; the compiled run prints 3 and 4 | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (walk) | `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex`, "Trait Types" | `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXNatSizeExclusionWalk.fss` | climb batch 5 rung Z | siblings: 402. Instantiation exclusion makes the two parameter types exclude each other, so the pair is a valid overloading. content.content:
- F-44 **The compiled checker enforces the multiple instantiation exclusion rule and relies on it, and the one library meets the rule.** The rule: no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait. The checker's Return Type Rule relies on it: with the rule relaxed alone, a program passes the checker and dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError` (`OverloadingOracle.scala:81-105`; the probe `ProbeMIEPick`). F-48 gives the kinds of static argument that the rule compares. Walk applies no instantiation exclusion: it accepts a type that extends two instantiations, and its overloading check does not count them as excluding (row 416; the review's section 3). P-43 keeps the rule. Besides the flat number tower of P-43, the library meets it by three changes of `952892a00`: `TotalComparison` extends `Comparison` and `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, no longer `StandardTotalOrder[\TotalComparison\]`; `AnyMaybe` extends `AnyUniqueItem` alone, no longer `Equality[\AnyMaybe\]` beside it; and `andCondCombine` chooses `andRelCond` by a `typecase`, in place of a second `ANDCOND`. So under walk, a program's `p1 ANDCOND p2` of two relational predicates, conditions built from a relation over a generator, which `filter` fuses, is no longer itself a relational predicate (row 458). The distance holds no exclusion error (F-53). Detail: `reviews/multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md` sections 1 to 3; `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:121-123`, `:959`; `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4861-4867`.
- F-175 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values in every passage.** It builds P-60. Appendix I's entry "Traits with comprises clauses read at the level of values" records the change. A call whose argument's static type stands between two closed traits runs the declaration that covers its value. Where its declarations have no static parameters, its type is the intersection of its most specific declarations' return types. Appendix I names five places where the compiled path departs. The checker checks a `comprises` clause at the closed trait's immediate subtypes only (row 487). The code generator crashes on a method call on a result typed by that intersection (row 540). Where any declaration of the overload set has static parameters, the checker types such a call by one of its most specific declarations instead, a deliberate choice (row 543). The checker refuses the Meet Rule's example for closed traits when its declarations have static parameters (row 546). The checker's verdict on an overload set can depend on the components compiled before it in the same JVM (row 547). Detail: `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:3185-3240`, with the rows at `:1597-1606` and `:3446-3459`; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 8 and 9.
- F-76 **The compiled checker accepts the specification's `comprises` example of the Meet Rule (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "The Meet Rule for Functions") by a coverage check used only in overload checking, not in its subtype test, and types a call whose argument's static type lies below closed traits and above the types that they list by the intersection of the return types of its most specific declarations, when they tie without coercion.** It builds P-60, which reads `comprises` at the level of values: several declarations below two overloads serve as their meet if together they cover it. Open: coverage refuses a pair when a declaration that it compares has static parameters (row 546). In an accepted family that has any other generic declaration, such a call is typed by the head of a sort, which follows declaration order and can vary between runs, not by the intersection (row 543). That narrower scope than P-60's is a default. On the compiled path, a method call on a value typed by the intersection crashes the code generator (row 540), and a generic declaration instantiated at an intersection type dies as it loads (row 559). The checker checks a `comprises` clause only at the closed trait's immediate subtypes, so a type in another component below a generic subtrait escapes it (row 487). Its verdict on an overload set can depend on the components compiled before it in the same JVM (row 547). Gated by `compiler_tests/*Comprises*` and `*CoverageReturn*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-return-type-rule/decision-record.md` sections 3 and 4.
- F-142 **Walk checks at load the Meet Rule for Functional Methods per providing type.** A type provides what it declares and what it inherits, but not what its `override` declarations override. The check covers every trait, object and object expression. A type with static parameters is checked through one type that stands for all its instances (F-145). That check skips each pair of functional methods whose parameter types mention a static parameter, and each pair that a supertype whose type mentions one provides. Symbolic operators, such as `+` or `||`, are skipped, as the compiled checker skips them. Checked, they would refuse only `EmptyString`'s `||` at load, which one declaration clears (row 611; F-245, measured at `d212b2c1f`). Walk's other refusals at load are in the `fortress-repo` skill's `references/interpreter.md`. Gated by `tests/FunctionalMethodMeet*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-meet/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 7.
- F-145 **Walk refuses at load an object that leaves an inherited abstract method uncovered, an `override` that overrides nothing, and a generic type that breaks the Meet Rule for Functional Methods.** Bodies at narrower parameter types define an abstract method only where together they cover its parameter types, with `comprises` clauses read, as P-147 decides: each position is split through the clauses, and every combination of parts must lie inside one body. A search that does not settle refuses the object: a cycle, a symbolic or unreadable type, 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations. A generic object is not checked (row 665), and an object whose one covering definition has a static parameter of its own is refused (row 728). The compiled checker covers the same way, within the same bounds, except where a method has static parameters of its own (row 725). F-147 gives the `override` check and F-142 the Meet Rule's. Gated by `tests/AbstractMethod*Walk` (`AbstractMethodCoverUnsettledWalk` among them), `OverrideNothing*Walk` and `compiler_tests/AbstractMethodCoveredPairs`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-coverage/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 6; `compile-ladder/rung-duplicates-coverage/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 8.
- F-147 **Walk reads an `override` by the chapter's strict subtype, and checks the `override` of a trait, object or object expression with static parameters once, at its declaration.** The `fortress-repo` skill gives the rule's cases (`references/interpreter.md`, "What walk checks"). An object inherits nothing that a trait's `override` overrides, so an abstract `override` leaves it without a body (rows 614, 649). Where walk does not read a static parameter's bounds, it accepts an `override` over an inherited declaration whose types mention one (row 693). Gated by `tests/Override*Walk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-override/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-88 **The compiled checker reads what a trait or object provides by the traits chapter's inheritance, and checks an overriding declaration's return type against the one it overrides.** A type provides its own methods and its immediate supertypes', less those that an own declaration overrides or repeats in its parameter types. So an object below a trait that redeclares an inherited method abstract must define it. The code generator refuses `override` (row 650). Gated by `compiler_tests/Override*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-overloading/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-80 **The compiled checker judges two functional methods of one name, abstract declarations included, by the Meet Rule for Functional Methods in each type that provides both, unless their name is a symbol.** Such a type must provide their meet, compared without the `self` parameter. F-88 says what a type provides. An abstract functional method beside a concrete one in the same trait, with the same parameter types, is refused by the No Duplicates Rule. Unchecked: a pair that only an object expression provides (row 570), and every operator whose name is a symbol, such as `+`, `<`, `||` or a subscript, since the checker skips them (row 584; F-245 measures what the skip hides). It checks operators named by capitals, such as `CAP`, and eight named by words, `juxtaposition` among them. The checker's overloading memo is keyed on all the inputs of the check, so a pair accepted at the top level is not reused unchecked in a trait that provides it. Gated by `compiler_tests/FunctionalMethodMeet*`, and by the refusals that the specification asks for, `XXXFunctionalMethodMeetAbstractSibling` and `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstract`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-overloading-checker/REPORT.md` sections 5 and 7; `compile-ladder/rung-checker-abstract-callsite/REPORT.md` section 1.
- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.
- P-97 **The specification's examples that break the exclusion rule take the library's shapes, and each original stays, marked "Not allowed".** The Working Draft offered such examples as legal. Each now shows the shape that the library uses for the same thing, with the original beside it under the specification's own mark, "Not allowed". The specification states the rule, which it calls instantiation exclusion, once, in the two parts of Luchangco's Types chapter of 2012 (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`; P-25): `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` says which instantiations exclude each other, and `basic/traits.tex` says that a declaration may not extend two that do. The covariance example, a trait that extends other instantiations of itself, is rewritten and marked in the same way. Its callout adds one sentence: the type group's later design, in the same Types chapter, declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, which neither walk nor the compiled path implements (row 404 records the gap). The calculi of Appendix A keep their rules as the team wrote them, under a callout that they predate the rule.
- P-60 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values.** `trait S comprises { U, V }` says that every value of `S` is a value of `U` or of `V`. So another trait may stand between `S` and its listed types. The specification defines "covers" once: a type covers another when every value of the second is a value of the first. The Meet Rule gains a case for closed traits. Where the rule asks for a declaration at the meet of two overloads' parameter types, several declarations below both serve, if together they cover the meet. So a call whose argument's static type stands between closed traits and their listed types may have several most specific declarations. The call's type is the intersection of their return types, and the declaration that runs is unique only at run time. Why: the proof addendum (`reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md`) shows this sound for ground declarations, at calls that need no coercion. A ground declaration's types hold no type variable, and `G[\ZZ32\]` is ground. The addendum also asks that the checker use coverage only in its overloading rules, to accept an overload set and to justify a call's tie among several most specific declarations, and not in its general subtype test. A declaration with static parameters, whose instance dispatch must choose at run time, is outside the proof: one instance would have to meet every one of the return types at once. The typing by the intersection is not extended to it, and the specification states that boundary.
- P-44 **`AnyIntegral` stays closed by its `comprises` clause, and the compiled checker reads the clause as the team's 2012 texts do.** The library's `AnyIntegral`, whose `comprises` clause lists the five integer types `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`, stays closed. Beside the clause stays a comment in the team's `NOT YET` form, by which the team's library records a clause that it cannot write yet: here `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]`, whose `where` form is not built. `Integral[\I\]` extends `AnyIntegral` and is not in the list. The checker accepts such a generic trait below a closed trait when every type that the checker knows below it is listed. The clause's text in the library, and walk, stay as they are. Why: the team's 2012 texts, Luchangco's Types chapter and Welterweight, are its later word (P-25, P-26), and by them the clause is right as written. The rule leaves a hole that every way of closing `AnyIntegral` shares, except the team's 2008 way, a `comprises` clause on `Integral[\I\]` itself: a program's own subtype of `Integral`, declared in another component, is accepted although no listed type is above it. Row 487 records the hole, and this decision does not close it.
- P-147 **An object defines an inherited abstract method when its bodies of that name at narrower parameter types together cover the abstract method's parameter types.** That is, each value of the abstract method's parameter types is a value of one body's parameter types. A `comprises` clause counts as the compiled checker reads it, which is P-60's reading: a closed trait is covered by its listed types. A body at the abstract method's own parameter types is the plain case. This is the team's rule of 2012, in Steele's abstract-method check of the compiled checker and in the Covered rule of the Welterweight calculus (`Papers/Welterweight/`). So the team's `Library/Pairs.fss` and `ProjectFortress/tests/FileConversion.fss` stay valid: an object in each defines an inherited abstract operator once for each type that a `comprises` clause lists. Walk applies the same rule at load, and its earlier allowance of any one narrower body goes. The traits chapter's sentence, which admitted no narrower body, is revised in the specification's revision form (P-96). Row 725: the acceptance of some valid objects whose methods have static parameters of their own, which the checker and walk (row 728) refuse. Row 665: walk's check of generic objects, which its load check skips.
